concepts.def: One star, the Sun, together with the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun. The natural satellites (moons) that orbit those planets are part of the solar system too.
A large body that orbits the Sun. There are eight planets in our solar system. A planet does not produce its own light; it is seen because it reflects light from the Sun.
A body that orbits the Sun but is much smaller than the eight planets. Dwarf planets are part of the solar system; they orbit the Sun in their own right rather than orbiting a planet.
A natural body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun directly. The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. Moons are part of the solar system.
A body that releases energy from nuclear fusion in its core, so it emits its own light. Our solar system contains one star, the Sun; everything else in the solar system orbits it.
A galaxy is an enormous collection of stars held together by gravity. The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our Sun, and our whole solar system is only a small part of it.
A cloud of dust and gas in space. The Sun was formed from such a cloud, and every star begins its life cycle as one.
Every part of a nebula attracts every other part. This gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas together, so the cloud contracts and becomes denser and hotter at its centre.
The hot, dense object formed as gravity draws the dust and gas of a nebula together. It becomes a star once the temperature is high enough for fusion reactions to begin.

The joining together of light nuclei to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy. In a young star, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei. Fusion is not burning and it is not the splitting of nuclei.
The long, stable stage of a star's life, during which hydrogen is fused into helium. How long this stage lasts, and what follows it, is determined by the size of the star.

In a stable star the gravitational collapse acting inwards is balanced by the expansion due to fusion energy acting outwards. Because the two effects are equal and opposite, the star stays the same size.
The stage a star about the size of the Sun enters after the main sequence, when it swells to a far larger size and its surface glows red.
The small, very dense, hot remnant left behind when a star the size of the Sun sheds its outer layers at the end of the red giant stage.
What a white dwarf becomes once it has cooled so far that it no longer emits visible light. This is the final stage in the life cycle of a star the size of the Sun.
The stage entered after the main sequence by a star much more massive than the Sun. It expands to an even greater size than a red giant before the star explodes.
The explosion of a massive star at the end of its life. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, and the explosion distributes the elements throughout the universe.
The extremely dense remnant left at the centre after a supernova. This is the end point for a massive star that is not massive enough to form a black hole.
The remnant left after the supernova of the most massive stars. Its gravitational field is so strong that not even light can escape from it.

Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements: light nuclei fuse into successively heavier nuclei, up to iron. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, whose explosion then spreads all these elements throughout the universe.
The path of one body around another. Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

A man-made object placed in orbit around the Earth or another planet. Like a moon, it is held in its orbit by the gravitational force of the body it orbits; unlike a moon, it was built and launched by people.

concepts.term: Direction of the gravitational force in a circular orbit
concepts.def: For a body in a circular orbit the gravitational force acts towards the centre of the orbit, at right angles to the direction in which the body is moving.

Velocity is speed in a given direction. Because gravity acts at right angles to the motion in a circular orbit, it continually changes the direction of travel without changing how fast the body is going, so the velocity changes while the speed stays the same.

An orbit in which the speed and the radius are matched, so the body keeps circling at the same distance. For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes: a faster satellite must orbit at a smaller radius, a slower satellite at a larger radius.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes what our solar system contains?
options: One star and eight planets only; dwarf planets are not included
One star, eight planets, dwarf planets and their natural satellites
One star, nine planets and the dwarf planets that orbit them
Eight planets and their moons, with the Sun counted as a planet
mcqs.explain: This is exactly the membership the specification gives: the Sun, the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit it, plus the moons that orbit planets.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the moons in our solar system is correct?
options: They orbit the Sun, keeping pace with the nearest planet
They orbit planets, but they are not part of the solar system
They orbit the Sun, and each one is classed as a dwarf planet
They orbit planets, and they are part of the solar system
mcqs.explain: Natural satellites are moons that orbit planets, and the specification counts them as part of the solar system.

mcqs.q: How is our solar system related to the Milky Way galaxy?
options: The Milky Way is one of the galaxies inside our solar system
The solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
The solar system sits at the exact centre of the Milky Way
The Milky Way and the solar system are two names for one thing
mcqs.explain: The specification states that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy, which contains a vast number of stars.

mcqs.q: The Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. What pulled this cloud together?
options: The pressure wave from a nearby exploding star pushing it in
The gravitational attraction between the parts of the cloud
The magnetic attraction between the dust grains in the cloud
The energy released by fusion reactions already taking place
mcqs.explain: Every part of the nebula attracts every other part, and this gravitational attraction makes the cloud contract.

mcqs.q: As gravity draws the dust and gas of a nebula together, the material becomes denser and hotter. What does this eventually lead to?
options: The temperature becomes high enough for fusion reactions to start
The gas begins to burn, releasing energy by chemical reaction
The largest nuclei split apart, releasing energy by fission
The cloud cools again as it radiates the energy back to space
mcqs.explain: The contraction raises the temperature and density until hydrogen nuclei can fuse, which is how a star begins its life cycle.

mcqs.q: Which nuclear process releases the energy of a newly formed star?
options: Hydrogen nuclei fuse together to form helium nuclei
Large nuclei such as uranium split into smaller nuclei
Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to release heat and light
Helium nuclei break apart to form hydrogen nuclei
mcqs.explain: In a young star, light hydrogen nuclei join to form heavier helium nuclei, releasing energy.

mcqs.q: A main sequence star such as the Sun stays the same size for billions of years. Why?
options: Gravity no longer acts on the star once fusion reactions have started
The expansion caused by fusion is far stronger than the collapse
Gravity pulling it inwards is balanced by the expansion caused by fusion energy
The star has used up its hydrogen, so nothing can change its size
mcqs.explain: The star is in equilibrium: gravitational collapse inwards and expansion due to fusion energy outwards are equal and opposite.

mcqs.q: Suppose the energy released by fusion in a stable star suddenly fell. What would happen to the size of the star?
options: It would expand, because gravity acts outwards from the centre
It would stay the same, because gravity stops once fusion starts
It would stay the same, because the star's mass has not changed
It would contract, because gravity would then be unbalanced
mcqs.explain: With less outward expansion from fusion energy, the inward gravitational collapse is no longer balanced, so the star gets smaller.

mcqs.q: What determines the stages that a star passes through in its life cycle?
options: The size of the star when it forms
The surface temperature of the star
The colour the star appears from Earth
The age the star has already reached
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the life cycle of a star is determined by the size of the star.

mcqs.q: A star the size of the Sun comes to the end of its main sequence stage. Which sequence of stages follows?
options: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
White dwarf, then red giant, then black dwarf
Red giant, then supernova, then neutron star
Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole
mcqs.explain: A star the size of the Sun swells into a red giant, sheds its outer layers to leave a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf.

mcqs.q: The Sun will eventually run out of hydrogen in its core. What will it finally become?
options: A black hole, formed when its core collapses inwards
A supernova, which throws its outer layers outwards
A neutron star, left at the centre of the old star
A white dwarf, which then cools to form a black dwarf
mcqs.explain: The Sun is not massive enough to explode; after the red giant stage it leaves a white dwarf that cools into a black dwarf.

mcqs.q: A star much more massive than the Sun leaves the main sequence. Which sequence of stages follows?
options: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf as the star cools
Red super giant, then supernova, then a black hole in every case
Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
Red super giant, then neutron star, then supernova as it explodes
mcqs.explain: A massive star expands into a red super giant and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole.

mcqs.q: After a supernova, what decides whether the remnant left behind is a neutron star or a black hole?
options: The colour of the supernova flash
The surface temperature of the star
The mass of the star that exploded
The number of elements produced
mcqs.explain: The life cycle is determined by the size of the star: only the most massive stars leave a black hole, others leave a neutron star.

mcqs.q: Where are the naturally occurring elements heavier than iron produced?
options: In the main sequence stage of any large star
In the core of every star, along with iron
In the hot early Earth, soon after it formed
In a supernova, the explosion of a massive star
mcqs.explain: The specification states that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

mcqs.q: How do fusion processes inside a star lead to the formation of new elements?
options: Heavy nuclei split, so lighter elements build up in the core
Nuclei join, producing every element up to uranium in the core
Nuclei join to make heavier nuclei, building elements up to iron
Atoms react chemically, combining to form new elements
mcqs.explain: Fusion joins light nuclei into successively heavier ones, which is how the elements up to iron are made inside a star.

mcqs.q: The Earth contains elements such as gold and lead. How did these elements come to be in the material from which the Earth formed?
options: They were formed inside the Earth after it had cooled
They were made by fusion inside the Sun and blown out
They have existed since the universe began, unchanged
A supernova explosion spread them out across the universe
mcqs.explain: The explosion of a massive star distributes the elements throughout the universe, so later material already contains them.

mcqs.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. What keeps it in that orbit?
options: Nothing does; there is no force acting on it out in space
The gravitational force of the Earth acting on the satellite
Balanced forces: gravity inwards and a force outwards
The push of its engines, which are kept running all the time
mcqs.explain: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

mcqs.q: What do the Moon and a communications satellite orbiting the Earth have in common?
options: Both are kept in orbit by gravity
Both were launched into orbit by people
Both travel in orbit around the Sun
Both formed naturally with the Earth
mcqs.explain: A natural satellite and an artificial satellite are alike in orbiting a planet, held there by the gravitational force.

mcqs.q: A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady speed. Which statement about its motion is correct?
options: Its velocity is constant because its speed is constant
Its speed increases because gravity is always pulling on it
Its velocity changes because its direction keeps changing
Its speed and velocity both change as it goes round
mcqs.explain: Velocity is speed in a given direction, and gravity acting towards the centre continually changes the direction of travel.

mcqs.q: A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel at a greater speed. What must happen if the orbit is to stay stable?
options: The radius of its orbit can stay the same
The radius of its orbit must decrease
The radius of its orbit must increase
The mass of the satellite must increase
mcqs.explain: For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes; a faster satellite orbits at a smaller radius.
